content: 1. Maternal consent was obtained, and pregnancy follow-up was conducted by the same practitioner. Exclusion criteria included congenital immune system deficiency, congenital heart disease, low birth weight, early rupture of membranes, asthma diagnosed before the age of 5, and lack of follow-up visits. Participants were divided into two groups based on breastfeeding duration: more than 12 months and less than 12 months. Mothers were instructed to maintain records of all diagnoses for their children, which were documented by physicians using the ICD-10 coding system. 2. A cross-sectional study conducted by Azevedo in 2005 included preschool children aged 36 to 71 months, randomly selected from public health centers in a low-income area in Brazil. A total of 369 children were enrolled. Data on infant feeding practices and dietary habits were collected through a prevalidated questionnaire and a 24-hour recall diary. Oral examinations were performed, and children with one or more cavitated, filled, or missing smooth surfaces in primary maxillary anterior teeth were classified as having severe early childhood caries (SECC). Exclusion criteria included children with medical illnesses. 3. Bajaj (2017) conducted a prospective cohort study within an ongoing observational study at Mount Sinai Medical School, Canada, evaluating the relationship between glucose tolerance during pregnancy and metabolic function postpartum. Women were recruited before or after glucose challenge tests (GCT) and underwent a 3-hour, 100-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Study visits at 3 months, 1 year, and 3 years postpartum included questionnaires, physical examinations, and OGTTs. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into three groups: less than 3 months, 3–12 months, and more than 12 months. 4. Belfort (2013) analyzed data from Project Viva, a longitudinal cohort study in Massachusetts, enrolling pregnant women from 1999 to 2002. Exclusion criteria included multiple gestations, inability to answer questions in English, gestational age over 22 weeks at the first prenatal visit, plans to move before delivery, preterm birth (<34 weeks), and missing breastfeeding or cognitive data. Breastfeeding data were collected at 6 and 12 months, and outcomes at 3 years included receptive language (Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test) and visual-motor abilities (WRAVMA subtests). 5. Blix (2017) utilized data from two population-based pregnancy cohorts: the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC). Infant feeding information was collected via mailed questionnaires (MoBa) or structured telephone interviews (DNBC) when children were 6 and 18 months old. 6. Brakohiapa (1988) conducted a cross-sectional study involving 202 children aged 12–24 months at Princess Marie Louise Hospital in Accra, Ghana. Mothers were interviewed about weaning time and eating habits. Outcomes included malnutrition, defined by weight-for-age, length-for-age, and weight-for-length thresholds. 7. Inclusion criteria required full-term birth, absence of chronic health problems affecting growth, and parents of the same race. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as never, less than 3 months, 3–5 months, 6 months to 1 year, or more than 1 year. Outcomes included BMI z-scores and overweight status at age 5. 8. Burke (2005) analyzed data from the Western Australian Pregnancy Cohort Study, which recruited 2,860 participants between 16 and 20 weeks of gestation from 1989 to 1992. Breastfeeding categories included never, less than 4 months, 5–8 months, 9–12 months, and more than 12 months. Outcomes included adiposity, overweight status, and BMI z-scores. 9. Butt (2014) analyzed data from the Malmö Diet and Cancer Study, which included 17,035 women from 1991 to 1996. Breastfeeding duration was calculated for up to seven children, and 424 cases of breast cancer were analyzed. Exclusion criteria included prior breast cancer diagnosis, nulliparity, missing parity data, cancer in situ, bilateral breast cancer, and insufficient tissue for analysis. 10. Caleyachetty (2013) conducted a prospective birth cohort study in Mysore, India, following 585 children until age 5. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into intervals (e.g., 1–4 months, 5–8 months). Outcomes included high BMI (above the 90th percentile) and skinfold thickness at age 5. 11. Camurdan (2011) conducted a retrospective cohort study at Gazi University Hospital, Ankara, following infants from birth to age 4. Exclusive breastfeeding and total breastfeeding duration were recorded. Outcomes included BMI at 15 months, 18 months, 2 years, 3 years, and 4 years. 12. Chaffee (2014) followed a birth cohort in Porto Alegre, Brazil, as part of a cluster-randomized trial. Breastfeeding duration was recorded, and dental status was assessed at 38 months using WHO protocols, including non-cavitated lesions. 13. Cheraghi (2013) conducted a cross-sectional study of 385 children aged 3–6 years in Urmia, Iran. Exclusion criteria included chronic or congenital diseases and long-term hospitalization. Breastfeeding data were collected via questionnaires completed by mothers. Outcomes included underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obesity based on BMI percentiles. 14. Chetwynd (2017) analyzed data from the Black Women’s Health Study, a longitudinal cohort of 59,001 women aged 21–69 years, enrolled in 1995. Hypertension was defined by medication use or physician diagnosis. Breastfeeding duration and parity were recorded. 15. Choi (2017) analyzed data from the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) from 2010 to 2013. Women aged 19–50 years were included, excluding pregnant women and those with incomplete data. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups: ≤5 months, 6–11 months, 12–23 months, and ≥24 months. 16. Christensen (2020) used data from the Odense Child Cohort (OCC), including mothers who gave birth between 2010 and 2013. Breastfeeding data were collected weekly via SMS questionnaires. Outcomes included hospitalization due to infections, retrieved from the Danish National Patient Registry. 17. Cohen (2009) analyzed data from the Southern Community Cohort Study (SCCS), focusing on racial disparities in cancer outcomes. Participants aged 40–79 years were recruited from community health centers in the southeastern United States. Breastfeeding duration and parity were recorded. Outcomes included obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²). 18. Danforth (2007) conducted a prospective cohort study, but specific details were not provided in the text.
